newsitem.title: UK: U.S. stocks quiet in London trading.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks quiet in London trading.

text.p: U.S. stocks were quiet in London trading on Monday, with dealers here predicting a mixed opening on Wall Street after the Dow's recent record-breaking run.

They said a bout of profit-taking could be in order ahead of Tuesday's key inflation report, but added that unless the figures were stronger than expected there was no reason to think a major retreat was due anytime soon.

"I would expect the market to be quiet ahead of Tuesday's numbers," said one dealer. "After two days of big gains there could be some profit-taking...but the momentum is so strong I would expect the market to push even higher before it tops out."
He said the benign economic backdrop should continue to lure mutual fund cash into the market in coming weeks and months.

"We have had an unbelievable run with the market up 24 percent since its May lows and the S&P 500 is on 21 times trailing earnings, but the last time we had inflation and the budget deficit this low combined with such strong profits growth was the early 60s."
Other dealers also said there was little reason to expect a major Wall Street correction in the near term.
"The market is full of fully invested bears," said another dealer at a U.S. securities house here.

"It's a difficult market to be in and a difficult market to be out of...in three months' time, I would expect the market to be at the same level as it is now, but as long as mutual fund flows continue, the market should remain buoyant."

On Friday, the Dow leapt 70.57 points to a record close of 7,782.04, its sixth record close in succession. Treasury bonds also rose, with the benchmark 30-year issue up 9/16 at a four-month high of 98-5/8, to yield 6.73 percent.
Markets took heart from Friday's unexpected drop in producer prices, which further eased the risk of a rise in U.S. short-term interest rates.
No major U.S. economic pointers were due to be released today.

The next key pointer to the health of the world's biggest economy comes with Tuesday's consumer prices report for May, with economists expecting an overall rise of 0.2 percent and a similar increase in the underlying figure excluding volatile food and energy costs.
Tuesday also sees the release of industrial production and capacity utilisation figures for the past month.
